explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Samuel says, "I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you." He's standing there with the new king in front of everybody and saying it plain. He adds that he has walked before them from his youth until this day. That's a whole lifetime of showing up.

Close to the feel of it, but Samuel never says that. He says, "I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you." Nothing about being weak or tired, friend. I've got some blurry edges myself, and I'd never call myself weak either.

I get why you'd guess it, with all that gray hair. But Samuel never says he's ready to rest. He says, "I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you." Then he points back to how he has walked before them from his youth until this day.

Right on, baker. Samuel asks, "Whose ox or donkey have I taken?" and so on, then says, "Tell me, and I will restore it to you." He's ready to pay it all back. A man who offers that is either very clean or very brave, and I think it's both.

That's a fair guess, but it isn't in the text. Samuel says if anyone has something against him, "Tell me, and I will restore it to you." The promise is to make things right with whoever was hurt. Nothing about quitting, friend.

It sounds like something a leader would say, but Samuel doesn't say it. After listing the ox, the donkey, the cheating and the bribe, he promises, "Tell me, and I will restore it to you." He'd give back what he took, plain and simple.

Not quite, friend. The people answer, "You have not cheated us or oppressed us," and add that he hasn't taken anything from the hand of man. So the answer is False. Nobody stepped up with a complaint, and I'd have checked the back of the room twice.

That's it. The people reply, "You have not cheated us or oppressed us," and say he has not taken anything from the hand of man. Not one person raised a hand against him. After a lifetime of leading, that's a mighty quiet room.
Yes, baker. Samuel says the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought the fathers out of Egypt (1 Samuel 12:8). Aaron was Moses' partner in the job. Two leaders, one rescue.

Joshua was a real leader, but Samuel doesn't name him here. He says the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought the fathers out of Egypt (1 Samuel 12:8). Joshua, Moses' helper, shows up in the Bible's story a little later. Easy one to mix up, friend.

Caleb is a good name, but it's not the one Samuel uses. He says the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought the fathers out of Egypt (1 Samuel 12:8). Aaron is the partner in this line. Keep Caleb in your pocket for another passage.

That's right, baker. Samuel says, "But they forgot the LORD their God." They were brought out and settled in the land, and then they forgot Him. That's a hard turn, and I think Samuel wants them to hear it plainly.

Not this time, friend. Samuel says, "But they forgot the LORD their God." That comes right after he tells how the fathers were settled in the land. So the answer is True, and the trouble in the next verse comes from that.

Yes, baker. They cried out, "We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths." They owned it right there in the middle of the trouble. Then they asked to be delivered so they could serve Him.

explanations.answer: They had mocked the LORD's prophets
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. What they confess is, "We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths." Nothing about prophets. Their confession was about leaving the LORD for other gods.

explanations.answer: They had robbed the LORD's altar
explanations.explanation: That one isn't in the passage. The fathers say, "We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths." They confess leaving Him, not robbing anything. Close the cash drawer on that one, baker.

You got it, baker. Samuel says, "So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel." Samuel is the last name on the list. He just slips himself in at the end and keeps walking, and I'd have needed a drumroll.
Look again, friend. Samuel says, "So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel." That last name is his own. So the answer is True, and he says it without making a fuss.

That's the word, baker. Samuel says the LORD delivered them from the hands of their enemies on every side, "and you dwelt securely." Enemies on every side, and then safe. That's a good day's work, and it was the LORD's.
I see why you'd think it, with all those enemies. But Samuel says the LORD delivered them from their enemies on every side, "and you dwelt securely." The fear was over by then, friend.

That's a different picture than the text gives. Samuel says the LORD delivered them from their enemies on every side, "and you dwelt securely." Nothing about living apart from each other. They were safe.
Right, baker. Samuel says they asked for a king "even though the LORD your God was your king." They already had the best King there is. That's like walking past a full oven to go look for a candle.
That's kind of you, but Samuel doesn't say it. He says they asked for a king "even though the LORD your God was your king." Samuel was the prophet, not the king. The LORD was the one on the throne.

Kish isn't in this part of Samuel's speech, friend. He says they asked for a king "even though the LORD your God was your king." Kish, Saul's father, doesn't come into it. The LORD is the King he names.

Yes, baker. Samuel says if they fear the LORD, serve Him and obey His voice, and if both they and their king follow the LORD their God, "then all will be well." Notice the king is in that "if" too. Everybody follows, everybody's fine.

This one is True, friend. Samuel really does say, "If you fear the LORD and serve Him and obey His voice," and if both they and the king follow the LORD, "then all will be well." It's a real promise of good. Hang on to that part.

That's right. Samuel says, "then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers." It's a serious warning, and he says it plainly. The fathers' story he just told is the example.

A hand around them would sound cozy, wouldn't it, friend? But Samuel says, "then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers." Against is the word. He's warning them, not hugging them.

Beside is a gentle word, but it's not what Samuel says. He says, "then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers." He's pointing back to what happened to the fathers. The word is against.
Yes, baker. Samuel says, "I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain." And he points out it's the wheat harvest. Thunder and rain at harvest time is not what anybody orders.
That sounds like a bigger bakery disaster than the text gives. Samuel says, "I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain." No hail, no locusts, friend. Just thunder and rain at harvest.
Not here, friend. Samuel says, "I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain." He doesn't mention fire at all. The sign is thunder and rain, at the wheat harvest.

explanations.answer: The evil of asking for a king
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Samuel says it's so "that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king." The thunder and rain are the sign for it. It's a heavy word, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: The strength of their new king
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, but the text goes another way. Samuel says it's so "that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king." The sign isn't about Saul's strength, friend.

explanations.answer: The LORD's care for their fields
explanations.explanation: I can see the harvest on your mind, friend. But Samuel says it's so "that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king." That's the lesson of the thunder and rain.
Yes, baker. The text says, "all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." The thunder and rain came on the very day Samuel called. I think those people stood very still.
A nice word, but it's not the one the text uses. It says, "all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." Nobody's cheering in this scene, friend. They're scared.
There's no doubting after that sky, friend. The text says, "all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." The thunder and rain came on the day Samuel called, and the people feared.
That's right, baker. Samuel answers them, "Do not be afraid." The crowd was begging not to die, and the first thing out of his mouth is comfort. Then he goes on to tell them how to keep going.
Not what he says, friend. Samuel answers the scared people with, "Do not be afraid." Then he tells them to serve the LORD with all their heart. No sending them home.
The text doesn't have him say that. Samuel's first words to them are, "Do not be afraid." After that he tells them not to turn aside from following the LORD. Comfort comes first, baker.

Careful, friend, it's the other way around. Samuel says, "Even though you have committed all this evil, do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart." So the answer is False. He tells them to keep following.

That's right, baker. Samuel says, "Even though you have committed all this evil, do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart." He doesn't tell them to quit. He tells them to stay and serve with everything they've got.

explanations.answer: He was pleased to make them His own
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Samuel says the LORD will not abandon His people "because He was pleased to make you His own." It's about what He chose, not what they earned. That's good news for anybody who's ever burnt a batch.

explanations.answer: They had kept every one of His laws
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason, and honestly the passage just showed they hadn't. Samuel says the LORD will not abandon them "because He was pleased to make you His own." It rests on His pleasure, friend. Not on their record.

explanations.answer: Their offerings had always pleased Him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Samuel says the LORD will not abandon His people "because He was pleased to make you His own." The reason is that He chose them. Offerings aren't mentioned.

That's it, baker. Samuel says, "far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you." He won't stop praying for them. That's a promise from a man who knows how they just acted.
Judging is what Samuel did for years, but it isn't the word here. He says, "far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you." The word is praying, friend.
Nope, no battle in this verse. Samuel says, "far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you." He won't stop praying. That's the promise.

Close, friend, but it says both. Samuel warns, "But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away." So the answer is False. It's the people and the king together, and not only the king.

Yes, baker. Samuel says, "But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away." Both, not only the king. It's a serious ending, and this isn't the end of the story. There's more to come.
